# 2026-2910: technical mechanisms, design reasoning and revision boundaries

These notes distinguish published construction from team-stated intent and original engineering inference. Selected numerical values are reported source data, not independently reproduced measurements. The recommended tests have not been performed. A binder snapshot does not certify every competition version.

## Original BLITZ: two mirrored four-bar collectors

Version: BLITZ original. [PDF p5](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1jPf-aOGhz0dntoAgahFBgRhJiJv9rGpj/view?usp=sharing#page=5) · [PDF p8](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1jPf-aOGhz0dntoAgahFBgRhJiJv9rGpj/view?usp=sharing#page=8)

**Published construction:** Dual four-bars; X44 deployment at 79.37:1; separate X60 roller drives.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Collect sideways while passing; collapse under impacts.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** This is a coupled routing decision. Collecting on either side allows the chassis to translate across a fuel pile while its fixed shooter points toward the destination. That can recover some of the directional independence normally purchased with a turret. A four-bar can also move backward under a frontal impact, but only if the linkage, motor controller, chain and hard stops permit that motion. More joints create more wear locations, and both collectors consume the space that another architecture could use for a hopper. The second intake should therefore be evaluated by additional useful fuel delivered, rather than the visual symmetry of the mechanism.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Compare opposite-side sweep paths against turning a single-intake robot, including one damaged linkage and time to replace it.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## Original BLITZ: serpentine inventory and passing

Version: BLITZ original. [PDF p5](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1jPf-aOGhz0dntoAgahFBgRhJiJv9rGpj/view?usp=sharing#page=5) · [PDF p9](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1jPf-aOGhz0dntoAgahFBgRhJiJv9rGpj/view?usp=sharing#page=9)

**Published construction:** Serpentine conveyor, two X60 feeder motors, three X60 shooter motors; variable hood.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Use the alliance zone as storage for a passing-centered role.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** The low-storage concept treats the field as an external buffer. Its success requires the alliance to recover that buffered fuel at the right time and place. Passing capacity and scoring capacity are different services even when the same launcher performs both. A continuous serpentine can constrain fuel well but adds contact length, curved transitions and friction; a well-controlled ball path may still be unable to supply enough mass flow. This original brief must be read alongside the later rebuild account: a design rationale is evidence of a hypothesis, not evidence that the hypothesis met the team’s competitive targets.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Measure fuel moved to a recoverable location, residual path inventory, and scoring available after the passer returns; vary partner collection quality.

**Limits:** The brief describes a 25-fuel/s feed capability; the later account reports inadequate overall performance. Do not treat that number as an independently demonstrated match average.

## RE-BLITZ: strengthened slapdown

Version: RE-BLITZ rebuild. [PDF p7](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1r-6zR4afbr_BpeZfWwcM5XL1N74FjScI/view?usp=sharing#page=7) · [PDF p9](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1r-6zR4afbr_BpeZfWwcM5XL1N74FjScI/view?usp=sharing#page=9)

**Published construction:** Four-bar replaced by slapdown; 0.6-inch plates; #35 deployment chain; powered bottom roller.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Strength, service access and reliable full-speed acquisition.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** A single pivot simplifies the force path: an exposed roller loads its arms, pivot and hard stop without several moving links sharing the impact. That does not make it automatically more impact tolerant. The stronger arm and larger deployment chain need a corresponding chassis attachment and a stop that can react a collision without loading the gearbox teeth. Powering the lower contact also matters at the bumper transition: fuel can otherwise be caught between a moving upper roller and a stationary surface while the robot continues advancing. Plate stiffness and ball transport are separate improvements and should be tested separately.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Test a wall hit and an oblique corner hit, then remeasure roller alignment and deployment current; test full-speed pickup of worn fuel.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## RE-BLITZ: preserve width through the floor and tower

Version: RE-BLITZ rebuild. [PDF p7](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1r-6zR4afbr_BpeZfWwcM5XL1N74FjScI/view?usp=sharing#page=7) · [PDF p10](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1r-6zR4afbr_BpeZfWwcM5XL1N74FjScI/view?usp=sharing#page=10)

**Published construction:** Ten inclined floor rollers; four-X60 feeder; Teflon backing; enlarged four-wide path.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Remove restrictions between hopper and launcher.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** Adding a fourth release lane helps only if four lanes remain supplied. A floor feeding a narrow or irregular throat produces alternating bursts and starvation even when the drum has ample power. Inclination and backing determine the normal force and the direction in which fuel escapes when multiple balls arrive together. Low-friction backing reduces the energy lost to sliding while powered rollers maintain forward contact. An open path also needs a controlled final approach: a ball entering the launch contact at a variable velocity or height changes compression and the exit state. Diagnose the last few balls separately from the first dense volley.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Log feeder current, wheel speed and scored output through a full hopper; repeat with 5, 15 and 30 fuel and with deliberate asymmetric loading.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## RE-BLITZ: drum, hood rollers and flywheel recovery

Version: RE-BLITZ rebuild. [PDF p10](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1r-6zR4afbr_BpeZfWwcM5XL1N74FjScI/view?usp=sharing#page=10)

**Published construction:** Four-inch drum, 1.5-inch hood rollers, overdriven flywheel; team reports >30 fuel/s and a 34 maximum.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** High discharge rate with manageable shooter recovery.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** A drum’s useful contact surface is a distributed launch interface. If fuel encounters different compression along its width, the nominally identical lanes can launch at different speeds. Flywheel energy can cover short impulses while the motors replace average energy, but a dense volley still requires sufficient sustained electrical power. Surface condition, ball wear and hood contact determine how much of the wheel’s speed becomes translation versus spin. The reported rate is valuable as a team result; it does not establish accuracy, defended performance, battery condition or an all-match average. Copy the geometry only with a plan to characterize those conditions.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Measure per-lane velocity and accuracy before and after a long volley; log loaded battery voltage and recovery between successive shots.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## RE-BLITZ: expansion actuated by the intake

Version: RE-BLITZ rebuild. [PDF p7](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1r-6zR4afbr_BpeZfWwcM5XL1N74FjScI/view?usp=sharing#page=7) · [PDF p11](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1r-6zR4afbr_BpeZfWwcM5XL1N74FjScI/view?usp=sharing#page=11)

**Published construction:** Intake-driven hopper expansion; smooth internal sheet-metal joints; deployed one-way catchers.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Store useful inventory and feed it back toward the shooter.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** The expanding walls and intake form one mechanism state machine. A wall that expands independently without managing its overlap can create a ledge, trap fuel, or fight the intake during retraction. Smooth fasteners reduce snagging, while the deployed catches react loads that should not be carried continuously by the intake motor. A large hopper helps separate acquisition from discharge, giving the driver freedom to reposition. That freedom disappears if the final fuel cannot leave without a specific intake movement. The recommendation should therefore specify both the retained capacity and the emptying sequence.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Interrupt deployment halfway with a full hopper; test reverse motion, ball trapping at panel overlaps, trench travel and final-fuel evacuation.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## RE-BLITZ: mechanism readiness and fallback operation

Version: RE-BLITZ rebuild. [PDF p12](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1r-6zR4afbr_BpeZfWwcM5XL1N74FjScI/view?usp=sharing#page=12) · [PDF p13](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1r-6zR4afbr_BpeZfWwcM5XL1N74FjScI/view?usp=sharing#page=13)

**Published construction:** Shot gates, vision-based targeting, CANrange preload sensing and fixed-position manual fallbacks.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Coordinate feeding with the actual launch state.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** A high mechanical ceiling can be lost to premature feed. The feeder must distinguish an intentional firing pause from a jam, an empty hopper and a shooter that has not recovered. Readiness should use measured values with hysteresis rather than one noisy threshold. Manual known-position shots preserve a useful degraded mode when localization fails, but require practiced driver cues and a stable mechanical zero. A mechanism database needs this control contract because an intake, indexer and drum borrowed from different robots may otherwise disagree about who owns the next ball.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Disable one camera, introduce an empty-hopper sensor error and force a heading correction mid-volley; check the operator can recover predictably.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

Readiness should use measured values with hysteresis rather than one noisy threshold. Manual known-position shots preserve a useful degraded mode when localization fails, but require practiced driver cues and a stable mechanical zero. A mechanism database needs this control contract because an intake, indexer and drum borrowed from different robots may otherwise disagree about who owns the next ball.

technical_notes.construction: Separate roller motors turn the exposed collecting surfaces. Deployment motors move multi-link arms; the linkage carries the roller across the frame boundary. The original binder reports X44 deployment at 79.37:1 and X60 roller drives.

technical_notes.engineering_analysis: A four-bar can change roller height and fore-aft position together. Impact accommodation requires the whole linkage, transmission and hard stops to permit the intended motion. A flexible plate alone does not establish a reliable collapse mode. Two mouths also require a merge that does not oppose incoming streams. Operating reconstruction: Deployment sets the mouth outside the bumper; rollers catch fuel from either side and move it inward. The piece must remain supported as it leaves the collector. A collector reaching its angle target is not proof a ball entered the conveyor. Transfer limits: Transfer lateral acquisition only with the merge, support contact and deploy load path. Two-sided collection is not authorization for a partner-dependent passing architecture.

Release leaves the chassis at the hood-defined angle, while chassis yaw provides aim. Transfer limits: Borrow constrained transport only where its contact history suits the new piece. Using the bumper as a stop makes fabric thickness and bumper installation part of the collector geometry. A stronger chain cannot correct a mouth held too high by the bumper. Operating reconstruction: Lowering the arm opens the mouth and deploys storage. The leading roller pulls fuel toward the lower powered contact; that contact carries it beyond the bumper into the floor. The team release says the deployed collector rests on bumper fabric. Transfer limits: The powered lower contact and simple arm are independently useful. technical_notes.engineering_analysis: The panel changes where gravity returns balls. A rate gain attributed to its addition is evidence of a whole-path bottleneck, not proof that every hopper benefits from the same slope. The rear launcher and front enclosure form one flow volume. Operating reconstruction: A ball can arrive anywhere across the floor; successive rollers push it to the rising feeder. Balls hitting the front backing slide back toward the pickup region. During a pause the system must avoid packing fuel harder into an unavailable launcher. Transfer limits: Preserve width from storage to feeder and inspect low-fill starvation. technical_notes.title: Compare paths and iteration costs, not intake names
technical_notes.version_label: BLITZ original versus RE-BLITZ rebuild; inherited physical studies
technical_notes.construction: Two collectors approach the chassis from opposite sides. They feed a constrained serpentine path and a fixed-yaw launcher rather than a deep open bulk hopper. The launcher structure occupies one end of the base, while the four-bar links occupy side deployment space. The binder base image shows four corner drive modules and a lightened pan. Electronics under the pan require turning the robot over and removing its protective belly sheet according to the team release; do not draw those electronics as accessible through the ball path. Battery removal direction is not established. A fixed launcher can aim with the chassis while the side collectors sweep laterally, but that is a control and route advantage, not unrestricted acquisition in every heading. The rebuild uses a single front slapdown collector, an expanding storage enclosure over an inclined roller floor, and a full-width raised shooter at the opposite end. Corner swerve modules sit below this path; the launcher side structure carries the drum and hood and attaches down toward the drive rails. Source dimensions give a 27.5 by 27-inch frame. The hopper panels and their joints surround the ball path, so screw heads on the hood can rub a sliding wall. A source reply specifically explains using flathead screws there. Some electronics moved above the brainpan, but under-pan equipment still needs underside access. Preserve that service split. Do not infer battery removal without its source view. Physical arrangement: The original places deployment links beside a constrained transport path. The rebuild allocates inventory volume and an active floor beneath it. Mouth deployment, stored inventory, launcher support and electronics access must be evaluated as one package; a compact intake alone says little about sustained feed. Piece path: Original: two collectors → constrained serpentine transport → fixed launcher. Rebuild: slapdown acquisition → bulk hopper/roller-floor path → launcher. Read both full physical studies; the original inlet merge and several rebuilt interfaces remain unknown.
technical_notes.team_stated_reason: Read typed premises for team explanations. Remaining causal analysis is editorial; it is not a claim about the team's intent.
technical_notes.engineering_analysis: Motions: Count collector deployment coordinates separately from roller motors, floor drive and hood motion. Two collectors do not automatically double throughput, and a single slapdown does not make the hopper feed problem disappear. Avoided: A less constrained bulk path can avoid repeated direction changes and dedicated conveyor transitions, if pieces can still reach the feeder consistently. Fewer deployment linkages may simplify impact recovery and replacement. Retained: Bulk inventory introduces bridging, starvation, compression and center-of-mass effects. An active floor adds contact and power demands. Rebuild development time is itself a cost; no numerical time saving or causal season improvement is established by the reviewed construction. Hypothesis: Evaluate pickup rate, usable stored capacity and sustained release together. A simple mechanism that starves the launcher cannot meet an elite throughput target. Conversely, a more elaborate collector that feeds no faster may spend space and iteration budget without useful benefit. Rival: The apparent improvement may depend on launcher changes, code, field strategy or testing maturity, rather than collector topology alone. Treat the before/after history as a source of hypotheses, not a controlled experiment. Reversal: A constrained path may win when orientation/order matters or bulk feed is unreliable. A bulk path may win when high inventory and simultaneous feed dominate. Select using the new game piece and geometry, not the historical team name.
technical_notes.recommended_validation: Before replacing an architecture, calculate capacity, clearances and bottleneck rates. Test the single most uncertain transfer or hopper-floor section only if its outcome can change the decision.
technical_notes.limitations: Common-condition rates, exact interface geometry, actual jam frequency and isolated effects of each redesign. Do not infer hidden plumbing or installed pairings from different binder snapshots. No controlled architecture comparison or individual cycle-time measurement performed.
technical_notes.review_scope: Selected captions/publications/code and inherited physical studies; not a controlled performance comparison.

context_documents.body:
> Physical evidence update 2026-11-07: read the complete [upgrade report](../PHYSICAL_UPGRADE_REPORT.md) and the new physical studies in `data/physical_studies.jsonl`. Earlier source accounts below retain their publication scopes.

# 2026-2910: technical mechanisms, design reasoning and revision boundaries

These notes distinguish published construction from team-stated intent and original engineering inference. Selected numerical values are reported source data, not independently reproduced measurements. The recommended tests have not been performed. A binder snapshot does not certify every competition version.

## Original BLITZ: two mirrored four-bar collectors

Version: BLITZ original. [PDF p5](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1jPf-aOGhz0dntoAgahFBgRhJiJv9rGpj/view?usp=sharing#page=5) · [PDF p8](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1jPf-aOGhz0dntoAgahFBgRhJiJv9rGpj/view?usp=sharing#page=8)

**Published construction:** Dual four-bars; X44 deployment at 79.37:1; separate X60 roller drives.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Collect sideways while passing; collapse under impacts.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** This is a coupled routing decision. Collecting on either side allows the chassis to translate across a fuel pile while its fixed shooter points toward the destination. That can recover some of the directional independence normally purchased with a turret. A four-bar can also move backward under a frontal impact, but only if the linkage, motor controller, chain and hard stops permit that motion. More joints create more wear locations, and both collectors consume the space that another architecture could use for a hopper. The second intake should therefore be evaluated by additional useful fuel delivered, rather than the visual symmetry of the mechanism.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Compare opposite-side sweep paths against turning a single-intake robot, including one damaged linkage and time to replace it.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## Original BLITZ: serpentine inventory and passing

Version: BLITZ original. [PDF p5](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1jPf-aOGhz0dntoAgahFBgRhJiJv9rGpj/view?usp=sharing#page=5) · [PDF p9](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1jPf-aOGhz0dntoAgahFBgRhJiJv9rGpj/view?usp=sharing#page=9)

**Published construction:** Serpentine conveyor, two X60 feeder motors, three X60 shooter motors; variable hood.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Use the alliance zone as storage for a passing-centered role.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** The low-storage concept treats the field as an external buffer. Its success requires the alliance to recover that buffered fuel at the right time and place. Passing capacity and scoring capacity are different services even when the same launcher performs both. A continuous serpentine can constrain fuel well but adds contact length, curved transitions and friction; a well-controlled ball path may still be unable to supply enough mass flow. This original brief must be read alongside the later rebuild account: a design rationale is evidence of a hypothesis, not evidence that the hypothesis met the team’s competitive targets.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Measure fuel moved to a recoverable location, residual path inventory, and scoring available after the passer returns; vary partner collection quality.

**Limits:** The brief describes a 25-fuel/s feed capability; the later account reports inadequate overall performance. Do not treat that number as an independently demonstrated match average.

## RE-BLITZ: strengthened slapdown

Version: RE-BLITZ rebuild. [PDF p7](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1r-6zR4afbr_BpeZfWwcM5XL1N74FjScI/view?usp=sharing#page=7) · [PDF p9](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1r-6zR4afbr_BpeZfWwcM5XL1N74FjScI/view?usp=sharing#page=9)

**Published construction:** Four-bar replaced by slapdown; 0.6-inch plates; #35 deployment chain; powered bottom roller.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Strength, service access and reliable full-speed acquisition.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** A single pivot simplifies the force path: an exposed roller loads its arms, pivot and hard stop without several moving links sharing the impact. That does not make it automatically more impact tolerant. The stronger arm and larger deployment chain need a corresponding chassis attachment and a stop that can react a collision without loading the gearbox teeth. Powering the lower contact also matters at the bumper transition: fuel can otherwise be caught between a moving upper roller and a stationary surface while the robot continues advancing. Plate stiffness and ball transport are separate improvements and should be tested separately.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Test a wall hit and an oblique corner hit, then remeasure roller alignment and deployment current; test full-speed pickup of worn fuel.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## RE-BLITZ: preserve width through the floor and tower

Version: RE-BLITZ rebuild. [PDF p7](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1r-6zR4afbr_BpeZfWwcM5XL1N74FjScI/view?usp=sharing#page=7) · [PDF p10](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1r-6zR4afbr_BpeZfWwcM5XL1N74FjScI/view?usp=sharing#page=10)

**Published construction:** Ten inclined floor rollers; four-X60 feeder; Teflon backing; enlarged four-wide path.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Remove restrictions between hopper and launcher.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** Adding a fourth release lane helps only if four lanes remain supplied. A floor feeding a narrow or irregular throat produces alternating bursts and starvation even when the drum has ample power. Inclination and backing determine the normal force and the direction in which fuel escapes when multiple balls arrive together. Low-friction backing reduces the energy lost to sliding while powered rollers maintain forward contact. An open path also needs a controlled final approach: a ball entering the launch contact at a variable velocity or height changes compression and the exit state. Diagnose the last few balls separately from the first dense volley.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Log feeder current, wheel speed and scored output through a full hopper; repeat with 5, 15 and 30 fuel and with deliberate asymmetric loading.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## RE-BLITZ: drum, hood rollers and flywheel recovery

Version: RE-BLITZ rebuild. [PDF p10](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1r-6zR4afbr_BpeZfWwcM5XL1N74FjScI/view?usp=sharing#page=10)

**Published construction:** Four-inch drum, 1.5-inch hood rollers, overdriven flywheel; team reports >30 fuel/s and a 34 maximum.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** High discharge rate with manageable shooter recovery.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** A drum’s useful contact surface is a distributed launch interface. If fuel encounters different compression along its width, the nominally identical lanes can launch at different speeds. Flywheel energy can cover short impulses while the motors replace average energy, but a dense volley still requires sufficient sustained electrical power. Surface condition, ball wear and hood contact determine how much of the wheel’s speed becomes translation versus spin. The reported rate is valuable as a team result; it does not establish accuracy, defended performance, battery condition or an all-match average. Copy the geometry only with a plan to characterize those conditions.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Measure per-lane velocity and accuracy before and after a long volley; log loaded battery voltage and recovery between successive shots.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## RE-BLITZ: expansion actuated by the intake

Version: RE-BLITZ rebuild. [PDF p7](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1r-6zR4afbr_BpeZfWwcM5XL1N74FjScI/view?usp=sharing#page=7) · [PDF p11](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1r-6zR4afbr_BpeZfWwcM5XL1N74FjScI/view?usp=sharing#page=11)

**Published construction:** Intake-driven hopper expansion; smooth internal sheet-metal joints; deployed one-way catchers.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Store useful inventory and feed it back toward the shooter.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** The expanding walls and intake form one mechanism state machine. A wall that expands independently without managing its overlap can create a ledge, trap fuel, or fight the intake during retraction. Smooth fasteners reduce snagging, while the deployed catches react loads that should not be carried continuously by the intake motor. A large hopper helps separate acquisition from discharge, giving the driver freedom to reposition. That freedom disappears if the final fuel cannot leave without a specific intake movement. The recommendation should therefore specify both the retained capacity and the emptying sequence.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Interrupt deployment halfway with a full hopper; test reverse motion, ball trapping at panel overlaps, trench travel and final-fuel evacuation.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## RE-BLITZ: mechanism readiness and fallback operation

Version: RE-BLITZ rebuild. [PDF p12](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1r-6zR4afbr_BpeZfWwcM5XL1N74FjScI/view?usp=sharing#page=12) · [PDF p13](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1r-6zR4afbr_BpeZfWwcM5XL1N74FjScI/view?usp=sharing#page=13)

**Published construction:** Shot gates, vision-based targeting, CANrange preload sensing and fixed-position manual fallbacks.

**Team-stated reason or evidence boundary:** Coordinate feeding with the actual launch state.

**Engineering analysis — original inference:** A high mechanical ceiling can be lost to premature feed. The feeder must distinguish an intentional firing pause from a jam, an empty hopper and a shooter that has not recovered. Readiness should use measured values with hysteresis rather than one noisy threshold. Manual known-position shots preserve a useful degraded mode when localization fails, but require practiced driver cues and a stable mechanical zero. A mechanism database needs this control contract because an intake, indexer and drum borrowed from different robots may otherwise disagree about who owns the next ball.

**Proposed validation — not a completed test:** Disable one camera, introduce an empty-hopper sensor error and force a heading correction mid-volley; check the operator can recover predictably.

**Limits:** The binder is a published configuration snapshot, not an independent durability or match-rate test.

## Selected published parameters

| Drive | Mk5n R2; X60 drive; X44 steer | [Source p7](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1jPf-aOGhz0dntoAgahFBgRhJiJv9rGpj/view?usp=sharing#page=7) |
| Intake | 79.37:1 deploy; mirrored four-bars | [Source p8](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1jPf-aOGhz0dntoAgahFBgRhJiJv9rGpj/view?usp=sharing#page=8) |
| Shooter | three X60 launch motors; one X44 hood | [Source p9](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1jPf-aOGhz0dntoAgahFBgRhJiJv9rGpj/view?usp=sharing#page=9) |
| Drive | 27.5×27-in frame; Mk5n R1 | [Source p8](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1r-6zR4afbr_BpeZfWwcM5XL1N74FjScI/view?usp=sharing#page=8) |
| Intake | 40:1 deploy; #35 chain; 2-in and 1.25-in rollers | [Source p9](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1r-6zR4afbr_BpeZfWwcM5XL1N74FjScI/view?usp=sharing#page=9) |

Version: BLITZ original versus RE-BLITZ rebuild; inherited physical studies

## Evidence premises

- **inherited_source_bounded_study**: Two collectors approach the chassis from opposite sides. They feed a constrained serpentine path and a fixed-yaw launcher rather than a deep open bulk hopper. The launcher structure occupies one end of the base, while the four-bar links occupy side deployment space. The binder base image shows four corner drive modules and a lightened pan. Electronics under the pan require turning the robot over and removing its protective belly sheet according to the team release; do not draw those electronics as accessible through the ball path. Battery removal direction is not established. A fixed launcher can aim with the chassis while the side collectors sweep laterally, but that is a control and route advantage, not unrestricted acquisition in every heading. Locator: data/physical_studies.jsonl#physical-2026-2910-original
- **inherited_source_bounded_study**: The rebuild uses a single front slapdown collector, an expanding storage enclosure over an inclined roller floor, and a full-width raised shooter at the opposite end. Corner swerve modules sit below this path; the launcher side structure carries the drum and hood and attaches down toward the drive rails. Source dimensions give a 27.5 by 27-inch frame. The hopper panels and their joints surround the ball path, so screw heads on the hood can rub a sliding wall. A source reply specifically explains using flathead screws there. Some electronics moved above the brainpan, but under-pan equipment still needs underside access. Preserve that service split. Do not infer battery removal without its source view. Locator: data/physical_studies.jsonl#physical-2026-2910-rebuild

## Piece flow

Original: two collectors → constrained serpentine transport → fixed launcher. Rebuild: slapdown acquisition → bulk hopper/roller-floor path → launcher. Read both full physical studies; the original inlet merge and several rebuilt interfaces remain unknown.

## Physical arrangement and swept space

The original places deployment links beside a constrained transport path. The rebuild allocates inventory volume and an active floor beneath it. Mouth deployment, stored inventory, launcher support and electronics access must be evaluated as one package; a compact intake alone says little about sustained feed.

## Independent motions and powered functions

Count collector deployment coordinates separately from roller motors, floor drive and hood motion. Two collectors do not automatically double throughput, and a single slapdown does not make the hopper feed problem disappear.

## Burdens avoided

A less constrained bulk path can avoid repeated direction changes and dedicated conveyor transitions, if pieces can still reach the feeder consistently. Fewer deployment linkages may simplify impact recovery and replacement.

Bulk inventory introduces bridging, starvation, compression and center-of-mass effects. An active floor adds contact and power demands. Rebuild development time is itself a cost; no numerical time saving or causal season improvement is established by the reviewed construction.

## Engineering hypothesis

Evaluate pickup rate, usable stored capacity and sustained release together. A simple mechanism that starves the launcher cannot meet an elite throughput target. Conversely, a more elaborate collector that feeds no faster may spend space and iteration budget without useful benefit.

## Rival explanation

The apparent improvement may depend on launcher changes, code, field strategy or testing maturity, rather than collector topology alone. Treat the before/after history as a source of hypotheses, not a controlled experiment.

A constrained path may win when orientation/order matters or bulk feed is unreliable. A bulk path may win when high inventory and simultaneous feed dominate. Select using the new game piece and geometry, not the historical team name.

## Unknowns

Common-condition rates, exact interface geometry, actual jam frequency and isolated effects of each redesign. Do not infer hidden plumbing or installed pairings from different binder snapshots.

Before replacing an architecture, calculate capacity, clearances and bottleneck rates. Test the single most uncertain transfer or hopper-floor section only if its outcome can change the decision.

No controlled architecture comparison or individual cycle-time measurement performed.

## Whole robot and packaging

The rebuild uses a single front slapdown collector, an expanding storage enclosure over an inclined roller floor, and a full-width raised shooter at the opposite end. Corner swerve modules sit below this path; the launcher side structure carries the drum and hood and attaches down toward the drive rails. Source dimensions give a 27.5 by 27-inch frame. ## Piece flow

The front collector lifts fuel across the bumper into the expanded hopper. Ten inclined rollers keep a broad stream moving toward the feeder. The backing panel returns piled fuel toward the shooter entry instead of allowing it to remain above the active floor. Feeder contacts lift and accelerate the stream; drum and powered hood contacts launch it. The full path must preserve width, not merely have a wide drum at the end. architecture_cases.piece_flow: Original: two collectors → constrained serpentine transport → fixed launcher. Rebuild: slapdown acquisition → bulk hopper/roller-floor path → launcher. Read both full physical studies; the original inlet merge and several rebuilt interfaces remain unknown.
architecture_cases.packaging: The original places deployment links beside a constrained transport path. The rebuild allocates inventory volume and an active floor beneath it. Mouth deployment, stored inventory, launcher support and electronics access must be evaluated as one package; a compact intake alone says little about sustained feed.
architecture_cases.independent_motions: Count collector deployment coordinates separately from roller motors, floor drive and hood motion. Two collectors do not automatically double throughput, and a single slapdown does not make the hopper feed problem disappear.
architecture_cases.burdens_avoided: A less constrained bulk path can avoid repeated direction changes and dedicated conveyor transitions, if pieces can still reach the feeder consistently. Fewer deployment linkages may simplify impact recovery and replacement.
architecture_cases.burdens_retained: Bulk inventory introduces bridging, starvation, compression and center-of-mass effects. An active floor adds contact and power demands. Rebuild development time is itself a cost; no numerical time saving or causal season improvement is established by the reviewed construction.
architecture_cases.engineering_hypothesis: Evaluate pickup rate, usable stored capacity and sustained release together. A simple mechanism that starves the launcher cannot meet an elite throughput target. Conversely, a more elaborate collector that feeds no faster may spend space and iteration budget without useful benefit.
architecture_cases.rival_explanation: The apparent improvement may depend on launcher changes, code, field strategy or testing maturity, rather than collector topology alone. Treat the before/after history as a source of hypotheses, not a controlled experiment.
architecture_cases.reversal_conditions: A constrained path may win when orientation/order matters or bulk feed is unreliable. A bulk path may win when high inventory and simultaneous feed dominate. Select using the new game piece and geometry, not the historical team name.
architecture_cases.unknowns: Common-condition rates, exact interface geometry, actual jam frequency and isolated effects of each redesign. Do not infer hidden plumbing or installed pairings from different binder snapshots.

source_reviews.title: Team 2910 Re•Blitz Tech Brief
source_reviews.locator: Strategical and Mechanical Reanalysis, Intake, Feeder and Shooter, Hopper, Software
source_reviews.review_basis: Downloaded original PDF and read extracted text
source_reviews.facts: Describes role pivot, single impact-resistant collector, floor and wide drum, as well as control fallback and reported rate.
source_reviews.limitations: Team measurements lack a complete independent protocol. Design goals and demonstrated outputs have separate scope.

source_review.whole_robot_explanation: Jack in the Bot initially built Blitz to move fuel continuously for its alliance, using the field as its inventory. Mirrored intakes made side-sweeping possible, and the low-storage path kept the focus on collecting and releasing during travel. The team’s own reanalysis says that intake and shoot-on-the-move limitations prevented this strategy from offsetting the loss of independent scoring, especially in autonomous and under defense. Re•Blitz changed the role and shortened the fuel path. The new robot combined a robust single collector, a buffer and a wide scoring burst while retaining a passing option.
piece_flow: Blitz’s independent four-bar intakes fed through side transition rollers into a serpentine path for immediate release.
Re•Blitz uses a slapdown collector with a powered lower contact to fill the hopper. Intake deployment pushes the hopper into position and retraction helps compact fuel.

A ten-roller inclined floor and compliant indexing roller present fuel four wide to the drum. The published software account describes sensor-based preload of the tower and a ready-to-score state before discharge.
source_review.packaging_and_motion: The 27.5 by 27-inch rebuild rotates modules to free space and packages major electronics around a central brainpan. The new hopper slides on bearings when the intake deploys and catches in the extended position, protecting the adjacent shooter from unintended return. It uses clear-enough tinted panels so inventory remains observable. The intake uses thicker side plates, a bash bar and split construction for service. Those are different solutions to impact tolerance and repair time.

subsystems.name: Collector and expanding hopper
subsystems.construction: Slapdown with bash bar, split side plates and powered lower rollers. Sliding one-piece polycarbonate hopper with retainers.
subsystems.operation: Intake deployment opens the hopper. Retraction compacts its contents toward the feed path.
subsystems.team_rationale: The team removed redundant intakes for storage volume and serviceability and emphasized impact resistance.
subsystems.engineering_analysis: A one-time expansion with catches makes initial deploy and reset decisive. Validate capture after asymmetric impacts and with a fully packed bin.
subsystems.interfaces: Collector travel and walls must clear the shooter and maintain feed alignment.
subsystems.service_and_failure_modes: Check catch engagement and the time to swap the exposed side plate or a bent lower roller.
subsystems.unknowns: No measured impact envelope or fielded variant chronology.

subsystems.name: Feeder and drum
subsystems.construction: Ten-roller floor at a reported 15-degree incline, compliant indexing roller, four-inch aluminum drum and overdriven flywheel.
subsystems.operation: Apply broad positive control and use sensor-based preload before the shot.
subsystems.team_rationale: Team preferred chains for lower rolling resistance in its arrangement and added guides to improve flow.
subsystems.engineering_analysis: Benchmark an equally supported belt or chain design with loaded tension and wear. Overall drive loss depends on more than transmission type.
subsystems.interfaces: Feed readiness, tower occupancy and heading gate work together.
subsystems.service_and_failure_modes: Check chain tension and empty-sensor behavior during partial blockage.
subsystems.unknowns: Loaded current and scoring conversion by range.

revisions: Original Blitz used two mirrored four-bar intakes, minimal storage and a serpentine transfer.
The team allocated three weeks for redesign, assembly and bring-up across the midseason rebuild.
Re•Blitz added a hopper, powered floor, four-wide launcher and low-friction guide boards. Team reports up to 34 BPS over a full hopper under its test conditions.
transferable_principles: Evaluate whether a partner-dependent role delivers enough fuel during autonomous and remains useful when the primary scorer is defended.
Reduce redundant acquisition when its service, packaging and tuning cost exceeds the additional usable fuel.
Record clear performance acceptance criteria before selecting a buffer size and feed width.
disconfirming_conditions: A high-speed passer can be superior when partner scoring is dependable and the playing area offers continuous fuel access.
A large loaded hopper can lose on a difficult route if fuel escapes, the collector catches or autonomous relocalization fails.
A high launch rate loses its value if pose gating leaves too little time to empty inventory.
remaining_gaps: No independent BPS or conversion logs, no authenticated event code and no complete comparison of rate versus fill level or battery state.
recommended_images: Original brief double-intake and serpentine pages. Re•Blitz brief intake, feeder and hopper pages for bash bar, four-wide path and passive deployment catches.
